title_en: Nobody Could Predict Jensen Huang — That Is Why Ordinary People Should Dollar-Cost Average
excerpt_en: Jensen Huang is back and U.S. stocks are going wild. But replay the last ten days: the president, the Treasury secretary and the board told three different stories, and nobody could have known the outcome. For ordinary people, the strategy that does not require prediction — dollar-cost averaging — is the one that fits.
body_en:
The moment the news of Jensen Huang's return landed, U.S. stocks went wild. Tech shares surged across the board, and the people who had been talking about a "technical bear market" days earlier changed their tune overnight.

But the point I want to make is the opposite one: from start to finish, nobody could have predicted how this played out.

Three different stories in a day — who dares claim they knew?

Replay the last ten days or so. On November 12, Jensen Huang resigned. Nvidia's first earnings report of the "post-Huang era" was actually spectacular: third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% year on year, with fourth-quarter guidance of $130 billion. The market shrugged anyway — because Huang said he was willing to come back, the board flatly refused, and the stock dropped about 14% in a single day.

Then came Treasury Secretary Bessent. He first took a hard line, demanding Nvidia find a new CEO from outside; on November 22 he softened on television, saying Huang's return had not been ruled out. Trump publicly backed Huang's return; the board said it would not consider it. The president, the Treasury secretary and the board were telling three different stories, changing by the day.

If the people sitting at the table do not know what the next card is, why would an ordinary person staring at a screen think they can call it?

News-chasers get hit from both sides

Every twist in those ten days was a meat grinder. Those who panic-sold on the resignation news sold right before the earnings surge. Those who chased the earnings ate the plunge after the board's refusal. Those who shouted "bottom" during the crash had to sit through the days when the Nasdaq hovered at the edge of a technical bear market. And those who rushed in only after the return was confirmed bought at the price of peak market euphoria.

It is not that they were not smart enough. Events like this simply cannot be known in advance. The second the news lands, the price has already moved. Ordinary people cannot match institutions on information speed or capital speed; betting your savings on an event that even the Treasury secretary has to walk back only ends with getting hit from both sides.

Dollar-cost averaging bets on time, not direction

My own approach is simple: dollar-cost average into the Nasdaq-100. No predictions, no market timing — buy when the day comes.

In this episode that approach looked "dumb": during the crash days the plan kept buying, into the decline; during the surge it bought only the scheduled amount, missing the chance to "go all in." But stretch the timeline out: the cheap shares bought during the plunge turned into profit the moment the return rally arrived, and buying less during the frenzy avoided loading up at the peak of sentiment. Dollar-cost averaging gives up the chance of "calling it right" in exchange for never missing the market entirely and never being shaken out by a single swing.

The ordinary investor's biggest enemy was never a return that is too low. It is the inability to hold on: panic-selling the dip, greedily chasing the rally, and ending up, years later, behind a machine that simply auto-debits every month.

Leave predictions to the gods

Whether Huang would come back, whether Nvidia's export-control reply due on November 25 will pass, what twist comes next — on questions like these, neither Wall Street's best analysts nor the most powerful people in Washington can give a straight answer.

If it cannot be predicted, stop trying to predict it. Dollar-cost averaging is the most suitable way for ordinary people to invest — not because it earns the most, but because it is the only approach ordinary people can actually stick with for years, and the one that reliably delivers the market's return.

Leave predictions to the gods. Keep the discipline for yourself.

Nothing here is investment advice.
